scenes.head: Present and future value
scenes.sub: An amount of money has a different value at every date. Learn to draw a timeline, discount single amounts with discount factors, move any amount to any date, cope with rates that change, and solve for the missing amount, rate or time, so that amounts at different dates can be compared fairly.

segs.say: Present and future value. An amount of money has a different value at every date. Learn to draw a timeline, discount single amounts with discount factors, move any amount to any date, cope with rates that change, and solve for the missing amount, rate or time, so that amounts at different dates can be compared fairly.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Construct a cash-flow timeline for a single-amount problem and match the rate per period to the spacing of the periods.
Calculate the present value of a future amount with a discount factor, for any compounding frequency and for amounts due between compounding dates.
Compare and combine amounts due at different dates by moving them to a common comparison date, including when the rate changes from period to period.
Find the unknown amount, rate or time in a single-amount problem with a formula, a financial calculator or a spreadsheet, and check the answer.
Explain why present value falls as the rate or the time rises, and why distant amounts are far more sensitive to the rate than near ones.

scenes.head: Two amounts of $10,000. Are they worth the same?

segs.say: It is March 2027, and Lantern Coffee Co. has been trading for a year. On Ana’s desk are two amounts, both of $10,000, and they are not worth the same.
One is cash in Lantern’s bank account today. The other is the $10,000 Lantern must repay Coastline Bank on 1 March 2028, when its two-year note matures.
Lantern borrowed in March 2026 at 6% a year. Rates have risen since then: a similar loan now costs 8% a year, compounded quarterly. Like everything about Coastline, that rate is fictional.
So what is next year’s repayment worth in today’s money? Less than $10,000. Working out how much less is what this lesson is about.

scenes.head: Move the repayment back one quarter at a time

segs.say: Draw the timeline first. Today, 1 March 2027, is quarter 0. The repayment sits four quarters away, at quarter 4. Interest is compounded quarterly, so the rate per quarter is 8% divided by 4, which is 2%.
Moving the amount back one quarter means dividing by 1.02. On 1 December 2027 it is worth $9,803.92.
Back another quarter, to 1 September: $9,611.69.
And to today: $9,238.45. That is the present value, $10,000 divided by 1.02 to the power 4.

Read it the other way round: $9,238.45 invested today at 2% a quarter grows to exactly $10,000 by 1 March 2028. The rest of this video shows why, and how to do the same for any amount, any rate and any pair of dates.

scenes.head: F00 introduced the two directions of time value.

segs.say: F00 introduced the two directions of time value. An amount today grows to a future value by compounding; an amount received later has a present value, found by discounting. They are one equation read in two directions:
FV = PV (1 + r)ⁿ ⇔ PV = FV/(1 + r)ⁿ

scenes.head: The equation links four quantities: the present value, the future value, the rate per period r and the number of periods n.

segs.say: The equation links four quantities: the present value, the future value, the rate per period r and the number of periods n. Know any three and you can find the fourth. Module 1 used it to grow money forward and to solve for the rate and the time. This lesson turns it round, to value amounts that arrive later, and stretches it to any pair of dates.

scenes.head: Every symbol must use the same period.

segs.say: Every symbol must use the same period. If interest is compounded quarterly, r is the rate per quarter and n counts quarters; if monthly, months. With a quoted annual rate (an APR) compounded m times a year, r = APR ÷ m and n = m × t, where t is the time in years. The lesson on effective annual rates explains why. Here it is the first step of every calculation.

scenes.head: A cash-flow timeline is a line marked off in periods, with time 0 at the date you are valuing from, usually today, and each amount written at the…

segs.say: A cash-flow timeline is a line marked off in periods, with time 0 at the date you are valuing from, usually today, and each amount written at the date it arrives. Drawing one takes ten seconds and prevents most time-value mistakes. It shows how many periods separate each amount from the date you care about, which way the amount has to move, and whether the rate matches the spacing. Amounts you receive are usually written above the line and amounts you pay below it, or with a minus sign.

scenes.head: For Lantern’s repayment, time 0 is 1 March 2027 and the periods are quarters, because the market rate is compounded quarterly.

segs.say: For Lantern’s repayment, time 0 is 1 March 2027 and the periods are quarters, because the market rate is compounded quarterly. The $10,000 sits at quarter 4, on 1 March 2028. The rate per quarter is 8% ÷ 4 = 2%. Moving the amount back one quarter means dividing by 1.02; moving it back four quarters means dividing by 1.02⁴.

Lantern’s $10,000 repayment moved back one quarter at a time at the March 2027 market rate of 8% a year compounded quarterly. Each step divides by 1.02; four steps give the present value on 1 March 2027.

scenes.head: In March 2027 the repayment is worth $9,238.45.

segs.say: In March 2027 the repayment is worth $9,238.45. Put the other way round, $9,238.45 invested today at 2% a quarter grows to exactly $10,000 by 1 March 2028, so a lender who can earn 8% compounded quarterly elsewhere would pay no more than that today for the right to receive the $10,000. The note also pays $150 of interest every quarter until then; the next lesson, on discounting cash flows, adds those payments and values the whole note.

scenes.head: The number 0.923845 is a discount factor: the present value of $1 received after n periods at a rate r per period, 1 ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ.

segs.say: The number 0.923845 is a discount factor: the present value of $1 received after n periods at a rate r per period, 1 ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ. Multiply any amount by it to bring the amount back to today. A discount factor is a price: at 2% a quarter, a dollar due in four quarters costs about 92.4 cents today. With a positive rate every factor lies between 0 and 1, and it shrinks as the rate rises or the wait lengthens.
Discount factors: the present value of $1 received after n years, at annual rates

scenes.head: Read along a row and the factor falls with time; read down a column and it falls with the rate.

segs.say: Read along a row and the factor falls with time; read down a column and it falls with the rate. The two effects compound together. At 2% a dollar due in 30 years is worth about 55 cents today; at 12%, just over 3 cents. That is why distant amounts barely count when rates are high, and why long-lived decisions, such as pensions, buildings and power plants, depend so heavily on the rate used to discount them.

scenes.head: Why present value falls as r or n rises

segs.say: Why present value falls as r or n rises. A present value is the amount that would grow into the future sum. A higher rate makes money grow faster, so less is needed today. A longer wait gives the money more periods to grow, so again less is needed today. The present value never reaches zero, but for long waits at high rates it comes close.

scenes.head: Discounting the repayment at 8% compounded once a year would give 10,000 ÷ 1.08 = 9,259.26, about $21 more, because 8% compounded annually is a lower…

segs.say: Discounting the repayment at 8% compounded once a year would give 10,000 ÷ 1.08 = 9,259.26, about $21 more, because 8% compounded annually is a lower effective rate than 8% compounded quarterly, which is 8.243216% a year. Either route gives the right answer as long as the rate and the periods match: discount at 2% a quarter for 4 quarters, or at the effective annual rate for 1 year, 10,000 ÷ 1.08243216 = 9,238.45.

chapters.title: Moving an amount to any date

scenes.head: Present value is a special case of a more general rule.

segs.say: Present value is a special case of a more general rule. An amount X at period j is worth X(1 + r)^(k − j) at period k. If k is later than j, the exponent is positive and the amount is compounded forward; if k is earlier, the exponent is negative and the amount is discounted back. The date you move everything to is the comparison date (some textbooks call it the focal date). It need not be today.

scenes.head: Why choose another date?

segs.say: Why choose another date? Because that is sometimes where the question lives. A business rescheduling a debt wants the single payment, at a new date, that is worth the same as the payments it replaces; a saver wants to know what a deposit will be worth at retirement. As long as one rate applies throughout, the choice of comparison date never changes which of two options is worth more. Moving every amount from one date to another multiplies all their values by the same factor.
Three offers compared at two dates, at 6% a year compounded annually

scenes.head: The $9,000 in two years is worth the most at either date, by a whisker: $9.97 more than $8,000 today and $12.58 more at year 4, the same gap grown by…

segs.say: The $9,000 in two years is worth the most at either date, by a whisker: $9.97 more than $8,000 today and $12.58 more at year 4, the same gap grown by 1.262477. The $10,000 in four years, the largest sum, is worth the least. The values change with the date; the ranking does not.

chapters.title: Replacing payments: the equation of value

scenes.head: When a borrower and a lender agree to replace one set of payments with another, the new payments must be worth the same as the old ones at the agreed…

segs.say: When a borrower and a lender agree to replace one set of payments with another, the new payments must be worth the same as the old ones at the agreed rate. Writing that condition at a comparison date gives an equation of value: the old payments, each moved to the date, add up to the same total as the new payments, each moved to the same date. Any date gives the same answer. The convenient one is usually the date of the unknown payment, because it then needs no factor.

scenes.head: Suppose a borrower owes $3,000 in one year and $4,000 in three years, and the lender agrees to take one payment X at year 2 instead, at 5% a year.

segs.say: Suppose a borrower owes $3,000 in one year and $4,000 in three years, and the lender agrees to take one payment X at year 2 instead, at 5% a year. At year 2 the first debt is a year overdue, so it is compounded once; the second is a year early, so it is discounted once: X = 3,000 × 1.05 + 4,000 ÷ 1.05 = 3,150 + 3,809.52 = 6,959.52. Written at time 0 instead, the equation is X ÷ 1.05² = 3,000 ÷ 1.05 + 4,000 ÷ 1.05³, which gives the same $6,959.52. Never add the two debts as they stand: $7,000 mixes dollars from different dates.

scenes.head: Nothing in the formula requires n to be a whole number.

segs.say: Nothing in the formula requires n to be a whole number. An amount due in 7 months, discounted at 6% compounded quarterly, is 7 ÷ 3 = 21/3 quarters away, so its discount factor is 1.015^(−7/3) = 0.965856. The same factor comes from the effective annual rate, 1.015⁴ − 1 = 6.1364%, applied for 7/12 of a year, because (1.015⁴)^(7/12) = 1.015^(7/3).

scenes.head: In practice lenders do not always compound over part of a period.

segs.say: In practice lenders do not always compound over part of a period. Some charge simple interest for the fraction, and the day-count convention (actual/365, 30/360 and others) varies by market and by contract, as the lesson on simple and compound interest explains. When a contract fixes the convention, follow it to the cent. For valuing and comparing amounts, the fractional exponent is the standard approach and the one this course uses.

chapters.title: When the rate changes over time

scenes.head: The single-rate formula assumes the same rate in every period.

segs.say: The single-rate formula assumes the same rate in every period. Often the rate changes: a bank resets a variable savings rate, and markets charge different rates for different horizons. The rule generalises directly. An amount is multiplied by the growth factor of each period it passes through, whatever that period’s rate. Over periods with rates r₁, r₂, …, rₙ, the future value is PV(1 + r₁)(1 + r₂)…(1 + rₙ), and a present value divides by the same product.

scenes.head: The Sandpiper Online savings account Ana plans to use shows why it matters.

segs.say: The Sandpiper Online savings account Ana plans to use shows why it matters. Its variable rate was 3.2% compounded monthly in 2026 and is now 3.6% (both fictional). A fictional saver who left $10,000 in an account like it for six months at 3.2% and then six months at 3.6% would end the year with 10,000 × (1 + 0.032/12)⁶ × (1.003)⁶ = 10,345.35 dollars. No single quoted rate describes that year; the right summary is the constant rate that gives the same product of factors.

scenes.head: That constant rate is a geometric mean: [(1 + r₁)(1 + r₂)…(1 + rₙ)]^(1/n) − 1.

segs.say: That constant rate is a geometric mean: [(1 + r₁)(1 + r₂)…(1 + rₙ)]^(1/n) − 1. For a three-year deposit paying 4%, 5% and 6%, the growth factor is 1.04 × 1.05 × 1.06 = 1.15752, and the equivalent constant rate is 1.15752^(1/3) − 1 = 4.9968%, a shade below the simple average of 5%. When interest rates move gently the gap is tiny. When returns swing, it is large: a fund that gains 20% and then loses 10% averages 5% a year arithmetically, but $1,000 becomes 1,000 × 1.2 × 0.9 = 1,080 dollars, the same as 3.923% a year for two years. Growth factors multiply; rates do not add.

scenes.head: Markets often quote a different rate for each horizon: one rate for money borrowed for a year, another for five years.

segs.say: Markets often quote a different rate for each horizon: one rate for money borrowed for a year, another for five years. Discounting each amount at the rate for its own horizon is the same idea, and later courses on bonds develop it.

scenes.head: Because the equation links four quantities, there are four kinds of single-amount problem.

segs.say: Because the equation links four quantities, there are four kinds of single-amount problem. The table collects them, with the rate and the number of periods always measured in the same period.
The four single-amount problems

scenes.head: Module 1 explains the root and the logarithm.

segs.say: Module 1 explains the root and the logarithm. Two habits matter here. First, check every answer by substituting it back: 9,400 × 1.042113^(1.5) should return $10,000. Second, check its size. A rate above 50% a year or a wait of three hundred years usually means a slip, such as a percentage typed as a whole number or months mixed with years.

scenes.head: Financial calculators and spreadsheets solve the same equation.

segs.say: Financial calculators and spreadsheets solve the same equation. A financial calculator has keys for the number of periods (N), the rate per period (I/Y, entered as a percentage), the present value (PV), a level payment (PMT) and the future value (FV): enter any four and compute the fifth. For a single amount the payment is zero. Calculators also have settings for payments and compounding periods a year; this course always works with the rate per period, so set both to 1 or follow your model’s manual.

scenes.head: Two conventions catch people out.

segs.say: Two conventions catch people out. Calculators and spreadsheets treat money you receive as positive and money you pay as negative, so the present value and the future value of one deal carry opposite signs; enter both as positive when solving for a rate or a time and you get an error. In a spreadsheet, =PV(0.02, 4, 0, 10000) returns −9,238.45: the amount you would pay today to receive $10,000 after four quarters. =FV(rate, nper, pmt, pv), =RATE(nper, pmt, pv, fv) and =NPER(rate, pmt, pv, fv) solve for the other unknowns, with pmt set to 0. Whatever the tool, the rate must be the rate per period that matches nper.

chapters.title: How sensitive is a present value to the rate?

scenes.head: The further away an amount is, the more its present value moves when the rate changes.

segs.say: The further away an amount is, the more its present value moves when the rate changes. Raise the rate from 5% to 6% a year and the present value of $1,000 due in one year falls from $952.38 to $943.40, by 0.94%. Due in ten years, it falls from $613.91 to $558.39, by 9.04%. Due in thirty years, from $231.38 to $174.11, by 24.75%. The fall grows with the wait, almost in proportion over short waits and a little less over long ones. This is why the values of long-term bonds, pension promises and distant business cash flows swing so much more with interest rates than the values of near ones.

scenes.head: Future value of a single amount

segs.say: Future value of a single amount: FV = PV (1 + r)ⁿ.
FV: Future value: what the amount is worth after n periods ($).
PV: Present value: the amount today (time 0) ($).
r: Interest rate per period, as a decimal (per period).
n: Number of periods; need not be a whole number (periods).
It assumes this: One rate in every period; interest is added each period and left to earn interest; nothing is paid in or taken out.
The rate and the periods must match: a quarterly rate with a number of quarters.

scenes.head: Present value and the discount factor

segs.say: Present value and the discount factor: PV = FV/(1 + r)ⁿ = FV × DFₙ, DFₙ = 1/(1 + r)ⁿ.
PV: Present value: what the future amount is worth today ($).
FV: The amount received after n periods ($).
DFₙ: Discount factor: the present value of $1 received after n periods.
r: Discount rate per period, as a decimal: the return available elsewhere at similar risk (per period).
n: Number of periods until the amount is received (periods).
It assumes this: One amount at a single date; one discount rate throughout.
A higher rate or a longer wait gives a smaller discount factor and so a smaller present value.

scenes.head: Rate per period and number of periods from a quoted annual rate

segs.say: Rate per period and number of periods from a quoted annual rate: r = APR/m, n = m t, PV = FV(1 + APR/m)^(−m t).
r: Rate per compounding period, as a decimal (per period).
APR: Quoted (nominal) annual rate, as a decimal (per year).
m: Compounding periods per year (2 semi-annual, 4 quarterly, 12 monthly) (per year).
n: Number of compounding periods (periods).
t: Time until the amount is received (years).
PV: Present value ($).
FV: The future amount ($).
It assumes this: Interest is compounded m times a year at APR ÷ m each time.
Equivalently, discount at the effective annual rate for t years: PV = FV ÷ (1 + EAR)ᵗ.

scenes.head: Value at any date (moving an amount)

segs.say: Value at any date (moving an amount): Vₖ = X (1 + r)^(k − j).
Vₖ: Value of the amount at the comparison date, period k ($).
X: The amount, which falls due at period j ($).
r: Rate per period, as a decimal (per period).
j: The period when the amount falls due (periods).
k: The comparison date (periods).
It assumes this: One rate throughout.
A positive exponent compounds forward; a negative one discounts back. Amounts may be added only once they are at the same date (the equation of value).

scenes.head: Changing rates and the equivalent constant rate

segs.say: Changing rates and the equivalent constant rate: FV = PV (1 + r₁)(1 + r₂)…(1 + rₙ), r̄ = [(1 + r₁)(1 + r₂)…(1 + rₙ)]^(1/n) − 1.
FV: Value at the end of period n ($).
PV: Value at time 0 ($).
rᵢ: Rate in period i, as a decimal (per period).
n: Number of periods (periods).
r̄: The constant rate per period that gives the same growth (a geometric mean) (per period).
It assumes this: Each period’s rate applies to the balance at the start of that period.
The equivalent constant rate is below the arithmetic average of the rates unless all the rates are equal.

scenes.head: Solving for the rate or the number of periods

segs.say: Solving for the rate or the number of periods: r = (FV/PV)^(1/n) − 1, n = (ln (FV / PV))/(ln (1 + r)).
r: Rate per period, as a decimal (per period).
n: Number of periods (periods).
PV: Amount at time 0 ($).
FV: Amount after n periods ($).
It assumes this: PV and FV have the same sign here (in a calculator or spreadsheet, enter them with opposite signs).
ln is the natural logarithm; any base works if used in both the top and the bottom.

chapters.title: Example: What a promised gift is worth today

scenes.head: What a promised gift is worth today

segs.say: A donor promises a fictional university $50,000 in six years. The university’s endowment earns 5% a year compounded semi-annually, and it uses that rate to value pledges. What is the pledge worth today?

scenes.head: What a promised gift is worth today

segs.say: Step 1. Draw the timeline and match the rate to the periods: compounding is semi-annual, so r = 5% ÷ 2 = 2.5% per half-year and n = 2 × 6 = 12 half-years.
Step 2. Discount factor: DF₁₂ = 1 ÷ 1.025¹² = 0.743556 (keep at least six decimal places).
Step 3. Present value: 50,000 × 0.743556 = 37,177.79 dollars, rounded to the cent only at the end.

Step 4. Check by compounding forward: 37,177.79 × 1.025¹² = 50,000.00. For comparison, annual compounding at 5% would give 50,000 ÷ 1.05⁶ = 37,310.77: more frequent compounding means a higher effective rate and so a lower present value.

scenes.head: What a promised gift is worth today

segs.say: About $37,177.79 today.

The pledge is not worth $50,000 to the university now: invested at the endowment’s rate, $37,177.79 would grow to the same amount. When it compares the pledge with gifts paid now, it should use the present value.

scenes.head: Rescheduling two debts

segs.say: A fictional hotel owes its builder $40,000 due in one year and $60,000 due in three years. Both sides value money at 6% a year compounded semi-annually. (a) The hotel proposes a single payment at the end of year 2 instead. How much should it pay? (b) The builder would rather receive a round $100,000. When should that payment be made for the deal to be fair?

scenes.head: Rescheduling two debts

segs.say: Step 1. Timeline in half-years at r = 3%: $40,000 at period 2 and $60,000 at period 6. For (a) the comparison date is period 4, the date of the new payment.
Step 2. (a) Equation of value at period 4: the first debt is 2 periods overdue and the second 2 periods early, so X = 40,000 × 1.03² + 60,000 × 1.03⁻² = 42,436.00 + 56,555.75 = 98,991.75.
Step 3. (b) Value both debts at time 0: 40,000 ÷ 1.03² + 60,000 ÷ 1.03⁶ = 37,703.84 + 50,249.06 = 87,952.89 (to the cent, from the unrounded parts).
Step 4. (b) Solve for the number of periods that turns $87,952.89 into $100,000: n = ln (100,000 ÷ 87,952.89) ÷ ln 1.03 = 4.343 half-years.
Step 5. Convert to years and check: 4.343 ÷ 2 = 2.17 years, about 2 years and 2 months. Check (a) at time 0 as well: 98,991.75 ÷ 1.03⁴ = 87,952.89, the same value as the two debts.

scenes.head: Rescheduling two debts

segs.say: (a) $98,991.75 at the end of year 2. (b) A payment of $100,000 is fair about 4.34 half-years, or 2.17 years, from now.

The single payment is less than the $100,000 owed in total because most of the debt is moved earlier. A round $100,000 needs a later date to be fair. Both answers come from the same rule: put every amount at one date before comparing.

scenes.head: Setting aside the repayment

segs.say: Ana asks how much Lantern would need to put aside on 1 March 2027 so that, with interest, it has exactly $10,000 on 1 March 2028 to repay the note’s principal. Coastline offers two homes for the money (fictional rates): (A) a 12-month business certificate of deposit paying 4.2% a year, credited at maturity; (B) three-month deposits, rolled over each quarter, which pay 4.0% a year (1% a quarter) now. Ana expects the three-month rate to rise to 4.4% a year (1.1% a quarter) from 1 September 2027. How much must she set aside under each plan, and what is the risk in plan B?

scenes.head: Setting aside the repayment

segs.say: Step 1. Timeline: $10,000 is needed at quarter 4 (1 March 2028). Plan A is one annual period at 4.2%: 10,000 ÷ 1.042 = 9,596.93.
Step 2. Plan B has a different rate in different quarters, so multiply the growth factors: 1.01 × 1.01 × 1.011 × 1.011 = 1.042666. Set-aside: 10,000 ÷ 1.042666 = 9,590.80.
Step 3. Compare: if the forecast holds, plan B needs $6.13 less today. Its equivalent constant rate is 1.042666^(1/4) − 1 = 1.0500% a quarter, or 4.2666% a year effective, against the CD’s 4.2%.
Step 4. Test the risk: if the three-month rate stays at 1% a quarter instead, the amount set aside grows to only 10,000 × 1.01⁴ ÷ 1.042666 = 9,980.23, $19.77 short of the repayment.

scenes.head: Setting aside the repayment

segs.say: Plan A: $9,596.93, with the $10,000 certain. Plan B: about $9,590.80, which works only if rates rise as Ana expects; if they stay at 1% a quarter it leaves Lantern $19.77 short.

Rolling short deposits saves a few dollars if rates rise as forecast, but the CD fixes the answer in advance. For a debt that must be paid on a known date, a cautious treasurer locks the rate unless the expected gain is large. Both amounts are above the $9,238.45 the repayment is worth at the 8% market lending rate, because deposits earn less than loans cost: while the cash sits on deposit at about 4.2%, Lantern still pays 6% on the note, so saving up early for a repayment has a cost.

scenes.head: Present value of a single amount

segs.say: Start from Lantern’s repayment: $10,000 due in one year at 8% compounded quarterly. Lengthen the wait to 30 years, then raise the rate: watch the present value fall and the sensitivity row grow. Switch the compounding between 1 and 12 to see how little the frequency matters compared with the rate and the time. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Solve for the rate or the time

segs.say: Set an amount today and a target. The explorer gives the rate you would need to reach the target in the time available, and the time you would need at the rate you can earn. Check each answer by substituting it back into FV = PV(1 + r)ⁿ. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Present value of $100 received after t years

segs.say: The present value of $100 received after up to 40 years, at three rates. Compare how fast each curve falls. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Mismatching the rate and the periods

segs.say: Mismatching the rate and the periods. With 6% compounded monthly, the rate per period is 0.5% and a three-year wait is 36 periods. Using 6% for 36 periods, or 0.5% for 3 periods, gives nonsense. Write r and n in the same unit before you calculate.

scenes.head: Rounding the discount factor too early

segs.say: Rounding the discount factor too early. The present value of $15,000 due in three years at 9% is 15,000 ÷ 1.09³ = 11,582.75. Rounding the factor 1 ÷ 1.09³ = 0.772183 to 0.77 gives $11,550.00, and even 0.7722 gives $11,583.00. Published answers sometimes carry slips of this kind. Keep at least six significant figures in every factor and round only the final amount.

scenes.head: Adding amounts from different dates

segs.say: Adding amounts from different dates. A debt of $3,000 in one year plus $4,000 in three years is not “$7,000”. Move every amount to one comparison date first; then add.

scenes.head: Averaging changing rates

segs.say: Averaging changing rates. Rates of 4%, 5% and 6% over three years do not grow money at 5% a year: multiply the growth factors (1.04 × 1.05 × 1.06) and take the cube root, which gives 4.9968%. With returns that swing, such as +20% and −10%, the arithmetic average (5%) overstates the true rate (3.923%) badly.

scenes.head: Subtracting the interest instead of dividing

segs.say: Subtracting the interest instead of dividing. Taking 9% × 3 = 27% off $15,000 gives $10,950, and dividing by 1 + 0.27 gives $11,811.02. Neither is a compound present value. Discounting divides by (1 + r) once for every period: 15,000 ÷ 1.09³.

scenes.head: Entering PV and FV with the same sign

segs.say: Entering PV and FV with the same sign. Calculators and spreadsheets treat money paid as negative and money received as positive. Solving for a rate or a time with both entered as positive returns an error; give the amount you pay a minus sign.

scenes.head: Present values of single amounts sit behind many business decisions, often without anyone using the words.

segs.say: Present values of single amounts sit behind many business decisions, often without anyone using the words.

scenes.head: “Buy now, pay in a year.” A fictional furniture retailer advertises a $1,200 sofa with nothing to pay for twelve months.

segs.say: “Buy now, pay in a year.” A fictional furniture retailer advertises a $1,200 sofa with nothing to pay for twelve months. Its finance manager treats the offer as a price cut. Money costs the retailer about 9% a year (a fictional figure), so $1,200 received in a year is worth 1,200 ÷ 1.09 = 1,100.92 dollars today. The promotion gives away $99.08 a sofa, 8.26% of the price, before allowing for customers who pay late or not at all. A straight 5% discount would cost $60. On these numbers the “free credit” is the dearer promotion, and the manager can say by how much.

scenes.head: Settling a claim.

segs.say: Settling a claim. A fictional engineering firm owes a client $250,000 under a court judgment payable in three years, and offers $205,000 now to settle. The client’s adviser discounts at 6%, the return the client could earn on similarly safe investments: 250,000 ÷ 1.06³ = 209,904.82 dollars. The offer is about $4,905 short, so the client asks for $210,000. If there were a real chance the firm would not survive three years, the adviser would discount at a higher rate, as F00 explains for risky amounts, and $205,000 now would start to look attractive.

scenes.head: Rates that move.

segs.say: Rates that move. A treasurer who holds cash for a known future payment, such as a tax bill or a loan repayment, often rolls it over in short deposits. Each rollover earns whatever rate is then on offer, so the amount needed today is the payment divided by the product of the growth factors she expects, not by one rate raised to a power. When she cannot afford to come up short, she may lock in a single rate for the whole period instead, giving up any gain if rates rise in exchange for certainty.

scenes.head: Ana runs the same arithmetic on her own plan.

segs.say: Ana runs the same arithmetic on her own plan. She hopes to put down a $60,000 deposit on a flat in April 2032, five years away, and the Sandpiper Online account she will save in now pays 3.6% a year compounded monthly, 0.3% a month. If she had one lump sum to set aside today, she would need 60,000 × 1.003⁻⁶⁰ = 50,129.72 dollars; the other $9,870.28 would be interest. She has nothing like that: most of her savings went into Lantern, and her $6,000 emergency fund stays where it is. She will have to build the deposit month by month, and every monthly deposit has its own date and its own number of months to earn interest. Valuing a series of payments like that is the work of the next module, and planning Ana’s saving is the course project.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: FV = PV(1 + r)ⁿ and PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ are one equation linking four quantities; know three and you can find the fourth. The rate and the periods must match.
Draw a timeline: time 0 at the valuation date, each amount at its own date, periods matching the compounding.
A discount factor, 1 ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ, is the present value of $1. It falls as the rate or the wait increases, so present values fall too.
An amount X at period j is worth X(1 + r)^(k − j) at period k. Compare or add amounts only at one comparison date; with one rate, the ranking of options does not depend on which date you choose.
An equation of value sets old and new payments equal at a comparison date, which is how debts are rescheduled.
With changing rates, multiply the growth factors period by period; the equivalent constant rate is a geometric mean, below the arithmetic average.
Solve for the rate with a root and for the time with logarithms, or with RATE and NPER (pmt = 0), giving PV and FV opposite signs. Check every answer by substituting it back.
Distant amounts are far more sensitive to the rate: a rise from 5% to 6% cuts the value of $1,000 due in 30 years by about a quarter.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
